sword_marker_records.content_osis: <div sID="gen5474" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="12" osisID="1Sam.12" sID="1Sam.12"/> <div eID="gen5474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5475" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen5476" type="x-p"/> We left the general assembly of the states together, in the close of the foregoing chapter; in this chapter we have Samuel's speech to them, when he resigned the government into the hands of Saul, in which, I. He clears himself from all suspicion or imputation of mismanagement, while the administration was in his hands, <reference osisRef="1Sam.12.1-1Sam.12.5">ver. 1-5</reference>. II. He reminds them of the great things God had done for them and for their fathers, <reference osisRef="1Sam.12.6-1Sam.12.13">ver. 6-13</reference>. III. He sets before them good and evil, the blessing and the curse, <reference osisRef="1Sam.12.14-1Sam.12.15">ver. 14, 15</reference>. IV. He awakens them to regard what he said to them, by calling to God for thunder, <reference osisRef="1Sam.12.16-1Sam.12.19">ver. 16-19</reference>. V. He encourages them with hopes that all should be well, <reference osisRef="1Sam.12.20-1Sam.12.25">ver. 20-25</reference>. This is his farewell sermon to that august assembly and Saul's coronation sermon.

Samuel's Discourse to Israel. ( b. c. 1069.)
1 And Samuel said unto all Israel, Behold, I have hearkened unto your voice in all that ye said unto me, and have made a king over you. 2 And now, behold, the king walketh before you: and I am old and gray-headed; and, behold, my sons are with you: and I have walked before you from my childhood unto this day. 3 Behold, here I am: witness against me before the Lord , and before his anointed: whose ox have I taken? or whose ass have I taken? or whom have I defrauded? whom have I oppressed? or of whose hand have I received any bribe to blind mine eyes therewith? and I will restore it you. 4 And they said, Thou hast not defrauded us, nor oppressed us, neither hast thou taken ought of any man's hand. 5 And he said unto them, The Lord is witness against you, and his anointed is witness this day, that ye have not found ought in my hand. And they answered, He is witness.
Here, I. Samuel gives them a short account of the late revolution, and of the present posture of their government, by way of preface to what he had further to say to them, v. 1, 2 . 1. For his own part, he had spent his days in their service; he began betimes to be useful among them, and had continued long so: " I have walked before you, as a guide to direct you, as a shepherd that leads his flock ( Ps. lxxx. 1 ), from my childhood unto this day. " As soon as he was illuminated with the light of prophecy, in his early days, he began to be a burning and shining light to Israel; "and now my best days are done: I am old and gray-headed; " therefore they were the more unkind to cast him off, yet therefore he was the more willing to resign, finding the weight of government heavy upon his stooping shoulders. He was old, and therefore the more able to advise them, and the more observant they should have been of what he said, for days shall speak and the multitude of years shall teach wisdom; and there is a particular reverence due to the aged, especially aged magistrates and aged ministers. "I am old, and therefore not likely to live long, perhaps may never have an opportunity of speaking to you again, and therefore take notice of what I say." 2. As for his sons, " Behold " (says he), " they are with you, you may, if you please, call them to an account for any thing they have done amiss. They are present with you, and have not, upon this revolution, fled from their country. They are upon the level with you, subjects to the new king as well as you; if you can prove them guilty of any wrong, you may prosecute them now by a due course of law, punish them, and oblige them to make restitution." 3. As for their new king, Samuel had gratified them in setting him over them ( v. 1 ): " I have hearkened to your voice in all that you said to me, being desirous to please you, if possible, and make you easy, though to the discarding of myself and family; and now will you hearken to me, and take my advice?" The change was now perfected: " Behold, the king walketh before you " ( v. 2 ); he appears in public, ready to serve you in public business. Now that you have made yourselves like the nations in your civil government, and have cast off the divine administration in that, take heed lest you make yourselves like the nations in religion and cast off the worship of God.
II. He solemnly appeals to them concerning his own integrity in the administration of the government ( v. 3 ): Witness against me, whose ox have I taken? Observe,
1. His design in this appeal. By this he intended, (1.) To convince them of the injury they had done him in setting him aside, when they had nothing amiss to charge him with (his government had no fault but that it was too cheap, too easy, too gentle), and also of the injury they had done themselves in turning off one that did not so much as take an ox or an ass from them, to put themselves under the power of one that would take from them their fields and vineyards, nay, and their very sons and daughters ( ch. viii. 11 ), so unlike would the manner of the king be from Samuel's manner. (2.) To preserve his own reputation. Those that heard of Samuel's being rejected as he was would be ready to suspect that certainly he had done some evil thing, or he would never have been so ill treated; so that it was necessary for him to make this challenge, that it might appear upon record that it was not for any iniquity in his hands that he was laid aside, but to gratify the humour of a giddy people, who owned they could not have a better man to rule them, only they desired a bigger man. There is a just debt which every man owes to his own good name, especially men in public stations, which is to guard it against unjust aspersions and suspicions, that we may finish our course with honour as well as joy. (3.) As he designed hereby to leave a good name behind him, so he designed to leave his successor a good example before him; let him write after his copy, and he will write fair. (4.) He designed, in the close of his discourse, to reprove the people, and therefore he begins with a vindication of himself; for he that will, with confidence, tell another of his sin, must see to it that he himself be clear.
2. In the appeal itself observe,
(1.) What it is that Samuel here acquits himself from. [1.] He had never, under any pretence whatsoever, taken that which was not his own, ox or ass, had never distrained their cattle for tribute, fines, or forfeitures, nor used their service without paying for it. [2.] He had never defrauded those with whom he dealt, nor oppressed those that were under his power. [3.] He had never taken bribes to pervert justice, nor was ever biassed by favour for affection to give judgment in a cause against his conscience.
(2.) How he calls upon those that had slighted him to bear witness concerning his conduct: " Here I am; witness against me. If you have any thing to lay to my charge, do it before the Lord and the king, the proper judges." He puts honour upon Saul, by owning himself accountable to him if guilty of any wrong.
III. Upon this appeal he is honourably acquitted. He did not expect that they would do him honour at parting, though he well deserved it, and therefore mentioned not any of the good services he had done them, for which they ought to have applauded him, and returned him the thanks of the house; all he desired was that they should do him justice, and that they did ( v. 4 ) readily owning, 1. That he had not made his government oppressive to them, nor used his power to their wrong. 2. That he had not made it expensive to them: Neither hast thou taken aught of any man's hand for the support of thy dignity. Like Nehemiah, he did not require the bread of the governor ( Neh. v. 18 ), had not only been righteous, but generous, had coveted no man's silver, or gold, or apparel, Acts xx. 33 .
IV. This honourable testimony borne to Samuel's integrity is left upon record to his honour ( v. 5 ): " The Lord is witness, who searcheth the heart, and his anointed is witness, who trieth overt acts;" and the people agree to it: " He is witness. " Note, The testimony of our neighbours, and especially the testimony of our own consciences for us, that we have in our places lived honestly, will be our comfort under the slights and contempts that are put upon us. Demetrius is a happy man, that has a good report of all men and of the truth itself, 3 John 12 .

entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen5485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5486" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> And Samuel said unto the people, <hi type="italic">It is</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> that advanced Moses and Aaron, and that brought your fathers up out of the land of Egypt. <hi type="super">7</hi> Now therefore stand still, that I may reason with you before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of all the righteous acts of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , which he did to you and to your fathers. <hi type="super">8</hi> When Jacob was come into Egypt, and your fathers cried unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , then the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> sent Moses and Aaron, which brought forth your fathers out of Egypt, and made them dwell in this place. <hi type="super">9</hi> And when they forgat the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> their God, he sold them into the hand of Sisera, captain of the host of Hazor, and into the hand of the Philistines, and into the hand of the king of Moab, and they fought against them. <hi type="super">10</hi> And they cried unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and said, We have sinned, because we have forsaken the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and have served Baalim and Ashtaroth: but now deliver us out of the hand of our enemies, and we will serve thee. <hi type="super">11</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> sent Jerubbaal, and Bedan, and Jephthah, and Samuel, and delivered you out of the hand of your enemies on every side, and ye dwelled safe. <hi type="super">12</hi> And when ye saw that Nahash the king of the children of Ammon came against you, ye said unto me, Nay; but a king shall reign over us: when the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God <hi type="italic">was</hi> your king. <hi type="super">13</hi> Now therefore behold the king whom ye have chosen, <hi type="italic">and</hi> whom ye have desired! and, behold, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath set a king over you. <hi type="super">14</hi> If ye will fear the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and serve him, and obey his voice, and not rebel against the commandment of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , then shall both ye and also the king that reigneth over you continue following the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God: <hi type="super">15</hi> But if ye will not obey the voice of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , but rebel against the commandment of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , then shall the hand of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> be against you, as <hi type="italic">it was</hi> against your fathers. <div eID="gen5486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5487" type="x-p"/> Samuel, having sufficiently secured his own reputation, instead of upbraiding the people upon it with their unkindness to him, sets himself to instruct them, and keep them in the way of their duty, and then the change of the government would be the less damage to them. <div eID="gen5487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5488" type="x-p"/> I. He reminds them of the great goodness of God to them and to their fathers, gives them an abstract of the history of their nation, that, by the consideration of the great things God had done for them, they might be for ever engaged to love him and serve him. "Come," says he (<reference osisRef="1Sam.12.7">v. 7</reference>), "stand still, stand in token of reverence when God is speaking to you, stand still in token of attention and composedness of mind, and give me leave to reason with you." Religion has reason on its side, <reference osisRef="Isa.1.18">Isa. i. 18</reference>. The work of ministers is to reason with people, not only to exhort and direct, but to persuade, to convince men's judgments, and so to gain their wills and affections. Let reason rule men, and they will be good. He reasons of the righteous acts of the Lord, that is, "both the benefits he hath bestowed upon you, in performance of his promises, and the punishments he has inflicted on you for your sins." His favours are called <hi type="italic">his righteous acts</hi> (<reference osisRef="Judg.5.11">Judg. v. 11</reference>), because in them he is just to his own honour. He not only puts them in mind of what God had done for them in their days, but of what he had done of old, in the days of their fathers, because the present age had the benefit of God's former favours. We may suppose that his discourse was much larger than as here related. 1. He reminds them of their deliverance out of Egypt. Into that house of bondage Jacob and his family came down poor and little; when they were oppressed they cried unto God, who advanced Moses and Aaron, from mean beginnings, to be their deliverers, and the founders of their state and settlement in Canaan, <reference osisRef="1Sam.12.6">v. 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.12.8">8</reference>. 2. entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen5491" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Samuel Calls for Thunder; Samuel Encourages and Comforts Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1069.)</title> <div sID="gen5492" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> Now therefore stand and see this great thing, which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will do before your eyes. <hi type="super">17</hi> <hi type="italic">Is it</hi> not wheat harvest to day? I will call unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and he shall send thunder and rain; that ye may perceive and see that your wickedness <hi type="italic">is</hi> great, which ye have done in the sight of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , in asking you a king. <hi type="super">18</hi> So Samuel called unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> sent thunder and rain that day: and all the people greatly feared the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> and Samuel. <hi type="super">19</hi> And all the people said unto Samuel, Pray for thy servants unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God, that we die not: for we have added unto all our sins <hi type="italic">this</hi> evil, to ask us a king. <hi type="super">20</hi> And Samuel said unto the people, Fear not: ye have done all this wickedness: yet turn not aside from following the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , but serve the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> with all your heart; <hi type="super">21</hi> And turn ye not aside: for <hi type="italic">then should ye go</hi> after vain <hi type="italic">things,</hi> which cannot profit nor deliver; for they <hi type="italic">are</hi> vain. <hi type="super">22</hi> For the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will not forsake his people for his great name's sake: because it hath pleased the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> to make you his people. <hi type="super">23</hi> Moreover as for me, God forbid that I should sin against the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> in ceasing to pray for you: but I will teach you the good and the right way: <hi type="super">24</hi> Only fear the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and serve him in truth with all your heart: for consider how great <hi type="italic">things</hi> he hath done for you. <hi type="super">25</hi> But if ye shall still do wickedly, ye shall be consumed, both ye and your king. <div eID="gen5492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5493" type="x-p"/> Two things Samuel here aims at:— <div eID="gen5493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5494" type="x-p"/> I. To convince the people of their sin in desiring a king. They were now rejoicing before God in and with their king (<reference osisRef="1Sam.11.15">ch. xi. 15</reference>), and offering to God the sacrifices of praise, which they hoped God would accept; and this perhaps made them think that there was no harm in their asking a king, but really they had done well in it. Therefore Samuel here charges it upon them as their sin, as wickedness, <hi type="italic">great wickedness in the sight of the Lord.</hi> Note, Though we meet with prosperity and success in a way of sin, yet we must not therefore think the more favourably of it. They have a king, and if they conduct themselves well their king may be a very great blessing to them, and yet Samuel will have them perceive and see that their <hi type="italic">wickedness was great in asking a king.</hi> We must never think well of that which God in his law frowns upon, though in his providence he may seem to smile upon it. Observe, <div eID="gen5494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5495" type="x-p"/> 1. The expressions of God's displeasure against them for asking a king. At Samuel's word, God sent prodigious thunder and rain upon them, at a season of the year when, in that country, the like was never seen or known before, <reference osisRef="1Sam.12.16-1Sam.12.18">v. 16-18</reference>. Thunder and rain have natural causes and sometimes terrible effects. But Samuel made it to appear that this was designed by the almighty power of God on purpose to convince them that they had done very <hi type="italic">wickedly in asking a king;</hi> not only by its coming in an unusual time, in wheat-harvest, and this on a fair clear day, when there appeared not to the eye any signs of a storm, but by his giving notice of it before. Had there happened to be thunder and rain at the time when he was speaking to them, he might have improved it for their awakening and conviction, as we may in a like case; but, to make it no less than a miracle, before it came, (1.) He spoke to them of it (<reference osisRef="1Sam.12.16-1Sam.12.17">v. 16, 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">Stand and see this great thing.</hi> He had before told them to <hi type="italic">stand and hear</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.12.7">v. 7</reference>); but, because he did not see that his reasoning with them affected them (so stupid were they and unthinking), now he bids them <hi type="italic">stand and see.</hi> If what he said in a <hi type="italic">still small voice</hi> did not reach their hearts, nor his doctrine which dropped as the dew, they shall hear God speaking to them in dreadful claps of thunder and the great rain of his strength. He appealed to this as a sign: "<hi type="italic">I will call upon the Lord, and he will send thunder, will</hi> send it just now, to confirm the word of his servant, and to make you see that I spoke truly when I told you that God was angry with you for <hi type="italic">asking a king.</hi>" And the event proved him a true prophet; the sign and wonder came to pass. (2.) He spoke to God for it. Samuel called unto the Lord, and, in answer to his prayer, even while he was yet speaking, <hi type="italic">the Lord sent thunder and rain.</hi> By this Samuel made it to appear, not only what a powerful influence God has upon this earth, that he could, of a sudden, when natural causes did not work towards it, produce this dreadful rain and thunder, and bring them out of his treasures (<reference osisRef="Ps.135.7">Ps. cxxxv. 7</reference>), but also what a powerful interest <hi type="italic">he</hi> had in heaven, that God would thus <hi type="italic">hearken to the voice of a man</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.10.14">Josh. x. 14</reference>) and answer him <hi type="italic">in the secret place of thunder,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.81.7">Ps. lxxxi. 7</reference>. Samuel, that son of prayer, was still famous for success in prayer. Now by this extraordinary thunder and rain sent on this occasion, [1.] God testified his displeasure against them in the same way in which he had formerly testified it, and at the prayer of Samuel too, against the Philistines. <hi type="italic">The Lord discomfited them with a great thunder,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.10">ch. vii. 10</reference>. Now that Israel rebelled, and vexed his Holy Spirit, he turned to be their enemy, and fought against them with the same weapons which, not long before, had been employed against their adversaries, <reference osisRef="Isa.63.10">Isa. lxiii. 10</reference>. [2.] He showed them their folly in desiring a king to save them, rather than God or Samuel, promising themselves more from an arm of flesh than from the arm of God or from the power of prayer. Could their king <hi type="italic">thunder with a voice like God?</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.40.9">Job xl. 9</reference>. Could their prince command such forces as the prophet could by his prayers? [3.] He intimated to them that how serene and prosperous soever their condition seemed to be now that they had a king, like the weather in wheat-harvest, yet, if God pleased, he could soon change the face of their heavens, and persecute them with his tempest, as the Psalmist speaks. <div eID="gen5495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5496" type="x-p"/> 2. The impressions which this made upon the people. It startled them very much, as well it might. (1.) <hi type="italic">They greatly feared the Lord and Samuel.</hi> Though when they had a king they were ready to think they must fear him only, God made them know that <hi type="italic">he is greatly to be feared</hi> and his prophets for his sake. Now they were rejoicing in their king, God taught them to rejoice with trembling. (2.) They owned their sin and folly in desiring a king: <hi type="italic">We have added to all our sins this evil,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.12.19">v. 19</reference>. Some people will not be brought to a sight of their sins by any gentler methods than storms and thunders. Samuel did not extort this confession from them till the matter was settled and the king confirmed, lest it should look as if he designed by it rather to establish himself in the government than to bring them to repentance. Now that they were <hi type="italic">flattering themselves in their own eyes, their iniquity was found to be hateful,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.36.2">Ps. xxxvi. 2</reference>. (3.) They earnestly begged Samuel's prayers (<reference osisRef="1Sam.12.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">Pray for thy servants, that we die not.</hi> They were apprehensive of their danger from the wrath of God, and could not expect that he should hear their prayers for themselves, and therefore they entreat Samuel to pray for them.
